title: Willow and Cricket's Wonderful Surprise
markdown:
The Sunny Meadow Talent Show was the most exciting event of the year, and Willow the bunny and Cricket the canary were buzzing loudest. Willow’s ears had minds of their own: one flop, one perk, a secret chat. She wiggled her nose. “Cricket, we must win. Imagine a shiny trophy.”

Cricket, a puff of sunshine-yellow, puffed her tiny chest. “I’ve practised trills until my beak tickled. We’ll be spectacular.”

They were best friends. Talent shows made them wobble. They were not quite sure what they were good at.

“Juggling,” Willow bounced. “Three shiny red carrots.” She trotted off and came back pleased.

Cricket fluttered onto a daisy. “I’ll do loop-the-loops around them.”

Willow tossed. The first carrot rose as if it believed in her. The second argued. Up, and then oopsie-daisy: one on her nose, one on Cricket’s head, one under a fern where a beetle had been minding its own business. Ears drooped to the ground. She wished, for a moment, to vanish under the leaf. Wobbly when nervous. The beetle, unimpressed, moved house.

Cricket landed beside her, chirp softer. She nudged the nose-carrot away with a wingtip. “Don’t worry. Lots of talents in the world. We have used only one, and it was the slippery kind.”

“A singing duet. Your high notes. My happy hopping song.”

They stood on a stump that made a fine stage if you were not picky. Willow began, “Hoppity-hop, hop, hop.” Cricket got excited. She trilled and warbled with all her might, then found a higher note and fell in love with it. Willow could not hear herself. It was like whispering at a fair, if the fair were entirely birds. A squirrel put its paws over its ears, then took them off to be polite.

“I can’t hear my own song. A bird concert in my ears.”

Cricket landed on her head. “Oops. Sometimes my excitement flies away.”

“A little,” Willow whispered.

“Comedy, then. I’ll tell jokes. You laugh and make faces.”

Willow tried her best trying-to-laugh face, the one she used when a joke was still putting its shoes on. Cricket told a joke about a worm who could not tie its shoelaces. A small hee-hee. A joke about a cloud that forgot rain. A wobbly giggle that arrived late and sat in the wrong seat. Attentive squirrels and slow ladybugs only blinked. One squirrel whispered that it had not known worms wore shoes. The ladybugs conferred and decided to wait for the next act.

That was when the real trouble put on a hat. Arwel Badger, the talent-show host, had already boomed that if no one had a truly spectacular act by sunset, the prize would be Farmer McGregor’s giant prize-winning pumpkin. The sun was leaning toward the hedge.

Willow wrung her paws. “My act keeps changing. Juggle, sing, jokes. A fluffy feathery mess. What if we’re not talented enough for even a pumpkin?”

Cricket looked at Willow’s flat ears, then at the dipping light. Her bounce faltered. “We’re trying so hard to be something we’re not. And it isn’t working.”

An idea fluttered. “What if we don’t have an act?”

Willow’s head tilted. “No act? The pumpkin?”

“Not no act. Our own. What do we like when we’re not trying to be best, funniest, loudest?”

Willow thought of sweet clover in the damp corner by the ditch, of dewdrops she liked to sniff one by one, of sun on fur after rain, of Cricket’s happy chirps that did not need a trophy to be true. “We like being us. Hopping. Chirping. Friends. The days we forget there is a show.”

“Exactly. Hop and chirp. Not fancy. Us. We give up the giant pumpkin. Being ourselves feels better.”

Arwel Badger announced them. A warm meadow welcome. Willow’s tummy fluttered. Cricket gave a brave little nod.

Willow did not think of juggling or loud singing. She thought of her friend and of hopping, of the ditch clover and the days without a host. She hopped: not a show-off hop, a happy Willow hop that made one ear flop in time. Cricket did not empty her lungs. She chirped, soft as tiny bells, a phrase they had used a hundred unremarkable mornings. Hop matched chirp, a simple dance. A daisy nodded without being asked. Two more daisies, not to be left out, did a smaller nod. The meadow watched, and for once watching felt like joining.

Quiet. Then a squirrel giggled. A ladybug clapped tiny legs. Applause spread like good news.

They did not win first prize. Arwel stepped forward. “For our special award. The ribbon for Most Fun Ever goes to Willow the bunny and Cricket the canary.”

Ears shot up. Cricket fluttered. They had been themselves together. No pumpkin lecture. Only a ribbon, a bit of sun left, and two friends who had finally practised the right thing.
